name: query-object
intent: Represent a database query as an ordinary object that composes through the language's own constructs and is translated into SQL by an interpreter, so that queries can be built, stored, passed and reused independently of the tables and columns behind them.
problem: Fixed finder methods hide one statement each: an ad-hoc query with optional filters cannot be assembled without either duplicating finders combinatorially or concatenating SQL strings, which spreads schema knowledge, dialect quirks and injection risk across every call site and leaves the query itself un-cacheable, un-testable and impossible to hand to another layer.
context: Data-access code over relational stores where queries are assembled from optional, reusable criteria (search forms, tenant scopes, report filters) and must run against one or more SQL dialects; typically paired with mapping metadata - table descriptors or an entity metamodel - that lets the query name classes and fields instead of tables and columns, and with a mapper that turns result rows back into domain objects.
benefits: Composability: predicates, joins and projections are values that combine with ordinary operators, so ad-hoc query variants are assembled from reusable parts instead of string concatenation.
Single point of change: table and column names live in mapping metadata, so a schema rename changes one declaration rather than every finder and every SQL string.
Safety: values travel as bind parameters attached to the query structure, removing the injection-prone practice of splicing values into SQL.
The query itself becomes storable and passable - it can be cached, serialised, compared or handed to a mapper or worker like any other object.
Dialect independence: the interpreter renders the same query for different databases, so callers do not commit to one backend.

Dynamic queries stay declarative: optional filters are added when present (filterOpt, apply_if, conditional where) without string assembly, and the composed query can be logged or asserted without a database.
tradeoffs: Indirection: a new API sits between the developer and SQL, and debugging requires the rendered statement, because what executes is not what was written.
Leaky abstraction: dialect features (window functions, CTEs, hints, vendor syntax) eventually need a raw escape hatch, so the abstraction is weakest exactly where queries get interesting.
Optimisation opacity: clause accumulation makes fan-out, missing indexes and accidental cross joins easy to produce and harder to review than one explicit statement.

Lifetime coupling: many realizations are session-bound (a JPA CriteriaQuery needs its EntityManager, a Core Data fetch request its context), so a stored query object cannot be shared across sessions or threads.
Execution overhead: building a tree and rendering SQL per call costs more than a constant string, so a compiled-statement cache keyed by query identity or shape becomes part of the design.
False confidence in tests: asserting the composed object rather than the rendered SQL can pass while the executed query is wrong.

participants.responsibility: The composable structure that describes the query - sources, joins, predicates, projection, ordering, limits - as data that can be stored, passed and reused.
Factory and composition surface that creates expressions and predicates and combines them (and/or/not) into new query objects; immutable composition returns new instances.
Walks the query object and renders a dialect-specific statement with bind parameters, resolving domain references through the mapping metadata.
Declares how classes and fields map to tables and columns (table descriptors, entity metamodel) so queries name the domain, not the schema; schema changes localise here.
Executes the rendered statement with its parameters, maps rows back to objects, and scopes statement caches and identity/unit-of-work state.

use_cases: Search and report screens where status, date-range or tenant filters are added only when the request supplies them.
Repository or DAO internals that build the same logical query for different stores or dialects.
Caching compiled statements by query shape or identity instead of rendering SQL per call.
Stored, reusable queries: named fetch-request templates, named queries or serialised filter trees that can be re-run unchanged.
Passing a query between layers or processes (controller to service to repository, or to a worker) without passing SQL text.
Testing query logic without a database: compose and assert the object, then execute one rendering as a smoke test.
Django applications pass unevaluated QuerySet objects through service or repository layers, chaining filter(), Q() and order_by() before evaluation at the boundary.
SQLAlchemy Core and ORM code composes generative Select objects with where(), join() and subqueries, then executes them through a Connection or Session for the target dialect.
Jakarta Persistence repositories use CriteriaBuilder and CriteriaQuery to build type-safe predicates, joins, ordering and parameters from optional search criteria.
avoid_when: One fixed statement per operation: a parameterised SQL constant or a prepared statement is simpler and equally safe.
Queries dominated by dialect-specific constructs (window functions, CTEs, hints): keep raw SQL with parameters and use a query object only for the dynamic part.
The stack already exposes one (EF Core IQueryable, ActiveRecord relations, SQLAlchemy select(), Kysely) - build on it instead of adding a second abstraction.
A small script or tool with two or three queries and no dynamic composition.
anti_patterns: A "query builder" that concatenates values into SQL - the object graph hides string interpolation and carries the injection risk with it.
One shared mutable query object that accumulates clauses between requests or threads.
Re-implementing a query DSL on top of a framework that already ships one (a hand-rolled builder over EF Core, Kysely or ActiveRecord relations).
Caching session-bound query objects (CriteriaQuery, fetch requests) beyond the session that built them.
Letting the abstraction leak: callers emit or inspect dialect SQL instead of composing, so schema knowledge is duplicated again.
design_principles: Single responsibility: composition, rendering and execution are separate collaborators.
Information hiding: schema knowledge is encapsulated in mapping metadata, not spread across call sites.
Open/closed: new criteria enter by composition, not by editing finder methods.
Dependency inversion: callers depend on the query abstraction, not on a SQL dialect.
Composition over inheritance: predicate trees combine, instead of a finder subclass per query variant.
best_practices: Bind values as parameters; never interpolate them into the statement text.
Keep composition immutable: each added criterion returns a new query object.
Render once per shape and cache the compiled statement by query identity or type.
Keep one explicit, parameterised raw-SQL escape hatch for constructs the abstraction cannot express.
Scope query objects to the session that built them; never cache them across sessions or threads.
Test the rendered SQL's semantics, not only the composed object, and log generated statements in development.
sources: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) - Query Object (chapter 13).
